sections.body:
Kaigo (介護) is support that helps a person live daily life according to their abilities and wishes. A person receiving services is called a riyōsha, not merely a collection of illnesses. Their needs include physical well-being, feelings, social relationships, habits, and meaning in life. Quick assistance is not necessarily appropriate if the person loses choices and opportunities to do things for themselves.

ADL means basic activities such as eating, dressing, transferring, bathing, and using the toilet. IADL includes more complex activities such as shopping, managing a schedule, and using transportation. QOL, or quality of life, asks whether life feels comfortable and meaningful to the person. These concepts help caregivers see needs as a whole.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Start by learning the person's habits: wake-up time, preferred foods, language, activities, and which body parts they can still use. Observe what they can actually do, then compare it with the care plan. Support may mean arranging the environment, giving a cue, supervising, or helping with only part of a task. Not every need calls for full assistance.

For example, a person may be able to comb their hair if the comb is placed in their right hand. Setting out the comb and mirror supports ability and confidence. A useful note describes the assistance needed and the person's response; do not write only “assistance provided.”

sections.body:
Dignity means that every person remains valued, including when they need full assistance. Using a preferred name, speaking to someone as an adult, and explaining actions are practical ways to show respect. Independence does not mean forcing someone to do everything alone. It also means making choices, expressing wishes, and receiving appropriate support.

Consent is a communication process, not just a single “yes.” Explain what you will do, why, and what choices are available in language the person can understand. Someone who has difficulty speaking can still show agreement or objection through movement, expression, and behavior. Check understanding and watch for changes in response throughout assistance.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
When helping someone change clothes, close the door or curtains and cover body parts that are not being cared for. Offer simple, genuine choices, such as blue or green clothing. Do not offer a choice you will not actually respect.

If a person refuses a bath, explore the reason: feeling cold or embarrassed, pain, fear of falling, or poor timing. Listen, offer an allowed alternative, and report to the team if the need remains unmet. Difficulty understanding a decision calls for team support, not a reason for the caregiver to make every decision alone.

sections.body:
Caregivers work as part of a team that may include nurses, doctors, social workers, therapists, dietitians, and service managers. Their main role is to support daily life, observe, document, and report changes. A shared plan helps staff provide consistent support. Competence and authority are set by workplace rules and training, not by a willingness to try something.

Confidentiality protects a person's identity, health information, family details, photos, and private conversations. Share information only with authorized people who need it for care. Discussing a person in an elevator, sending photos through a personal account, or sharing a story whose supposedly hidden identity is still easy to recognize can violate privacy.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
If an instruction is unclear, repeat its main point and ask for clarification before acting. When a task is outside your training, explain your limitation and contact the person in charge. Do not change medication, dosage, or clinical decisions on your own. Medication-related assistance must follow applicable rules, authority, and supervision.

Use the official record system, lock devices, and check recipients before sending reports. Requests for information from family members also require verification of identity and authority. Maintain a friendly professional relationship, while following facility policy on gifts, money, and personal matters.
sections.title: Applying the Procedures at Work

sections.body:
Abuse or neglect may include violence, insults, threats, neglecting needs, misuse of money, or violating bodily boundaries and privacy. Work pressure does not excuse these actions. People who have difficulty speaking or need full assistance still have the right to be heard and protected.

If you witness an incident or receive a complaint, prioritize safety and follow the safeguarding reporting process. Record what was said and the facts observed; do not investigate or draw conclusions yourself. Do not retaliate, blame the person, or promise secrecy that would prevent protection. Use supervision and team support when work pressure begins to affect staff behavior.

sections.body:
The body works as an integrated whole. The brain and nerves regulate movement, attention, and sensation; muscles, bones, and joints support posture and transfers. The heart and blood vessels circulate blood, the lungs support breathing, and the digestive system and kidneys process food and manage waste. A change in one function can affect how someone eats, walks, speaks, or uses the toilet.

Caregivers do not need to make a diagnosis to report useful observations. Compare today's condition with the person's usual condition: speech, facial color, breathing, appetite, activity, and elimination patterns. A person's concern is important information and should not be dismissed just because an examination appears normal.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Follow the sequence: look, listen, ask, and record. If assigned to measure vital signs, use the trained equipment and method and follow the facility's reporting thresholds. Include the time, circumstances, and symptoms with the readings; do not judge safety from one number alone.

Sudden changes such as difficulty waking, breathing difficulty, or new weakness require an immediate response under procedure. Do not conclude that it is “just old age.” Report the facts and call the responsible staff member before resuming a risky activity.

sections.body:
Listen to concerns about pain: its location, when it began, what the person was doing when it started, and the words they use. For someone who has difficulty speaking, observe changes in expression, movement, and response to assistance, then report them. Use an assessment tool only if assigned and trained to do so. Silence does not mean there is no pain, and caregivers must not change medication to treat it.

End-of-life support follows the team plan and choices communicated by the person or an authorized party under procedure. Caregivers support comfort, privacy, family relationships, and spiritual needs without imposing personal beliefs. Refusal to eat, changes in breathing, and new concerns must still be reported; do not respond with force or independent clinical decisions. A calm presence, attentive listening, and clear handover are important parts of support.

sections.body:
Aging may bring changes in strength, balance, vision, hearing, skin, and response speed. These changes vary from person to person. Age alone does not explain someone's abilities, interests, or decisions. Consider life history, the environment, conditions assessed by health professionals, and the assistance the person usually uses.

Losing a partner, moving home, or having fewer social roles can affect a person's sense of security and self-esteem. Someone may want to continue caring for plants or choosing clothes even when they need physical assistance. Opportunities to take part in meaningful activities support their life, rather than merely filling a care schedule.

Adjust lighting, reduce noise, put frequently used items within reach, and allow time to respond. Make sure glasses or hearing aids are used according to the person's wishes and plan. Do not automatically shout or speak as if to a child.

Observe new changes separately from familiar ones. Loss of appetite, withdrawal, or new pain should be reported to the team. Do not assume that every older person is forgetful, depressed, or unable to learn.

Disability may involve movement, vision, hearing, communication, or cognitive function. Barriers can also come from the environment: narrow doors, information that cannot be read, or equipment that is hard to reach. Good support reduces barriers and considers what the person wants to do.

Hemiparesis means weakness on one side of the body. Each person's condition and abilities differ, so the team assessment must identify the stronger side, pain, range of motion, and transfer method. Do not pull a weak arm or assume that side has no sensation. A speech impairment also does not automatically mean the person cannot understand a conversation.

When dressing someone with weakness on one side, a general principle is to dress the side needing assistance first and undress the easier side first. Adapt this to the plan, clothing, pain, and staff training. Explain each step and continue involving the person's usable hand or abilities.

Use visual cues, writing, pictures, or extra time for communication as needed. Place utensils, call bells, and chairs according to the person's assessment, not staff habits. Consult the team about changes to assistive devices.

sections.body:
Dementia is a condition that can affect memory, thinking, communication, and daily activities. It is not an inevitable part of aging. Health professionals make the diagnosis. For caregivers, the important thing is to understand the person's individual needs and help them feel safe, not test or embarrass them about their memory.

Difficulty remembering recent events may cause a person to repeat questions. Disorientation may cause confusion about place or time. Difficulty following a sequence may make clothing or equipment seem hard to use. Support responses should address observed barriers, not just a diagnostic label.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Use a familiar schedule, simple cues, and one-step prompts. If the person repeats a question about mealtime, answer calmly and point to the relevant cue. Do not force the person to admit that they have already asked the same question.

Support choices the person can still make, such as choosing a drink from two safe options. Consider their language, habits, and life history. Coordinate changes in support with the team so staff use a consistent approach and do not cause confusion.

Behavior that seems difficult is often a way of communicating a need that has not yet been understood. The person may feel afraid, lonely, embarrassed, uncomfortable, or confused. Before labeling them “difficult,” observe what happens before, during, and after the behavior. A noisy environment, staff changes, or instructions given too quickly may be relevant context.

Validating emotions means acknowledging feelings, not agreeing with every statement. If a person says they want to go home, a staff member might say that they seem to miss home and ask what would help them feel comfortable. A prolonged argument about the facts often does not help the relationship or safety.

Record the trigger, the person's words, the staff response, and the outcome. Try a simple approach: lower your voice, give the person space, offer an activity they enjoy, or explain again at a better time. Report suspected new physical needs or changes in condition to the team.

When a person wants to walk, use supervision and environmental adjustments as specified in the plan. Locking, tying up, or medicating someone for staff convenience is not a caregiver's decision. The team must address risk through procedures that respect the person's rights.

Sudden or fluctuating confusion must not immediately be treated as a familiar dementia pattern. Caregivers should report changes in attention, awareness, activity, or behavior to clinical staff. Their role is to observe and maintain safety; distinguishing clinical causes requires professional assessment.

Family members can help identify habits, preferred names, past occupations, and things that comfort the person. Use this information to personalize support. The person remains at the center of conversations and choices; family members are not automatically authorized to receive every private detail or make every decision.

When a change occurs, describe the person's usual condition, when they were last seen as usual, what has changed, and what actions have been taken. Ask for additional information only if doing so will not delay calling for help. Record observations without making your own diagnosis.

In conversations with family, ask open questions about routines and preferences. Repeat your understanding to confirm the information is accurate. Share concerns through the team and avoid promising outcomes that cannot be guaranteed. Staff should also discuss situations where family support and the person's wishes appear to differ.

sections.body:
Communication is more than giving instructions. Staff need to understand what the person feels, needs, and wants. Active listening involves attention, pauses, and restating the main point in one's own words. An open question such as “What feels uncomfortable?” gives the person more room than guessing at an answer.

Facial expression, gaze, posture, and movement can add to what is said. A grimace may indicate discomfort, but ask or report to clarify its cause. Silence does not always mean agreement. Do not interpret behavior based only on culture or age; confirm with the person and the team's information.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Sit or stand where the person can see your face without feeling intimidated. Introduce yourself, use the name they prefer, and reduce distractions. After they speak, summarize and ask whether you understood correctly. If they have difficulty speaking, use an agreed communication aid.

Do not rush to fill every pause. Give the person time to form an answer. While providing physical assistance, continue to observe their expression and ask whether they are comfortable. Record important words accurately instead of replacing them with assumptions such as “uncooperative.”

sections.body:
A good explanation of assistance says what will happen, why, and how the person can participate. Use everyday language before technical terms. Short sentences are easier to follow, especially when attention or hearing is limited. A calm tone and suitable pace are more helpful than a loud voice.

Directions should relate to the current action. “Let's hold this handrail” is easier to follow than several instructions at once. Avoid promises such as “it definitely won't hurt.” Instead, explain that the person can tell you if they feel pain or want to stop. Along with asking “Do you understand?”, invite the person to show or say what they understood.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Before assisting, explain the purpose and ask permission. As you proceed, explain the next action and wait for a response. If the person seems confused, explain again more simply, show the equipment, or demonstrate a safe movement. Do not force repetition in a way that embarrasses them.

Afterward, ask whether they are comfortable and place the call bell within reach. The person's feedback can guide future adjustments. In Japanese, use clear polite expressions; sentences that are too long or complicated keigo can make understanding harder.

Communication barriers may arise from language, hearing, vision, or difficulty expressing words. Choose support based on the person's needs. Large print helps some people, but not everyone can read well. Hearing aids also do not remove every difficulty, especially in a noisy room.

Caregivers learning Japanese need to distinguish an unfamiliar word from an unclear instruction. Nodding to hide a lack of understanding can lead to mistakes. Clarifying is part of professional work: ask for repetition, repeat the information back, or point out the term that needs confirmation. For important information, use an interpreter or approved support under policy.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

Speak where your face can be seen, at a comfortable distance, and in a clear voice. Do not shout from behind. If a person has difficulty expressing words, use yes-or-no choices or an agreed communication board while still checking their preferences. Do not assume a short answer means they do not want to take part.

When receiving instructions, repeat the time, name, quantity, and action. If anything is still unclear, stop before beginning a risky task. Note unfamiliar terms to study after work safety has been secured.

sections.body:
Infection prevention applies to every person receiving care, not only those known to be ill. Assess risk based on the task and possible contact with body fluids, broken skin, or contaminated objects. Hand hygiene and suitable protective equipment interrupt the transfer of contaminants between tasks.

Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Clean your hands using the facility method before and after contacts that require it and after removing gloves. Visibly dirty hands should be washed with soap and water. Additional rules for specific infections come from the responsible staff member; do not decide isolation measures on your own.

Keep clean and dirty workflows separate: prepare clean equipment before starting, place used items in designated locations, and do not touch door handles or phones with soiled gloves. Change gloves between people and when switching from a dirty task to a clean one.

Choose protective equipment based on the task assessment and your training. Follow the taught sequence for putting it on and removing it to avoid contaminating yourself. Use cleaning products, dilution, and contact times approved by the facility; do not mix cleaning chemicals.

sections.body:
Fall risk is affected by the person, the activity, and the environment. Wet floors, cables, poor lighting, unsuitable footwear, and equipment out of reach can increase risk. Urgent toileting needs or changes in condition also matter. An old assessment is not enough when circumstances change.

A near miss, or hiyari-hatto, is an incident that could have caused harm but did not result in injury. Reporting helps the team improve the system before an accident occurs. The main purpose is to understand causes and prevention, not find someone to blame. Record objective observations: what happened, where and when it happened, and the conditions at the time.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Check the walking route, equipment brakes where relevant, call bell, and placement of belongings before providing assistance. Make sure the assistive device matches the plan and the person knows how to request help. Do not remove opportunities to move simply because staff feel afraid; discuss safe approaches with the team.

If a person falls, do not immediately lift or pull them up. Call for help, make the area safe, and follow the facility's assessment and response procedures. Record the facts after immediate needs have been addressed. Repeated changes at a particular time or place may indicate that the plan needs adjustment.

sections.body:
In an emergency, staff must recognize danger, call for help, and follow trained procedures. Breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness, or a sudden change in function must be escalated immediately. Do not wait to make your own diagnosis. At work, learn the call buttons, contact routes, address, and person in charge on each shift.

A good call for help gives the location, the person's identity as recorded in the system, observed condition, time of the incident, and assistance needed. Mention any environmental danger as well. Emergency interventions such as resuscitation require hands-on training and current instructions; this app does not replace that training.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
During a fire or disaster, follow the facility evacuation plan and responders' instructions. Before an incident, learn the safe routes, assembly points, list of people receiving care, and their assistive-equipment needs. Avoid spontaneous actions that could add danger, such as taking a route that has not been declared safe.

After the incident, hand information over to the receiving team and record the factual sequence of events. Do not leave a person at risk unsupervised to look for documents; ask a colleague for help and divide tasks. Review drills regularly so the response does not depend on memorization alone.

sections.body:
Body mechanics use posture and movement to make work more stable. A secure base, staying close to the task, and avoiding twisting the back while carrying a load help reduce inefficient movement. However, body mechanics alone cannot make every transfer safe. The person's weight and abilities, available equipment and space, and number of staff still determine how assistance should be provided.

Handling a person is different from lifting an object. A person may move suddenly, feel pain, or lose balance. Follow the transfer assessment and equipment-use policy. Never lift a person who cannot support their own body alone just because a staff member feels strong enough.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

Before assisting, read the plan and check for changes in the person's condition. Make sure equipment is available, working, and suitable for the person. Using a hoist, sling, or transfer device requires specific training and a check that the equipment fits. Staffing must follow the assessment and device instructions, not an assumption that two people are always enough.

Explain how the person can participate and coordinate so one staff member leads the directions. If the situation does not match the plan, stop and request a reassessment. Feeling rushed or short-staffed is not a reason to skip checks.

Supine, side-lying, and sitting positions have different purposes and risks. A comfortable position must take into account the person's mobility, pain, breathing, and support plan. Use pillows or positioning aids according to the assessment; the goal is not simply to make the body look tidy.

Prolonged pressure, friction, moisture, and shear can damage skin. A person who has difficulty changing position needs a risk assessment and individual plan. No single repositioning schedule is automatically suitable for everyone. Follow the plan and report if it cannot be carried out or the person is uncomfortable.

When repositioning someone, protect their privacy and use trained methods to reduce friction. Do not drag the person by pulling on an arm or clothing. Make sure sheet folds, equipment, and body parts do not create unwanted pressure. Leave the call bell within reach when finished.

Observe the skin during care activities when possible and with consent. Report new redness, wounds, excess moisture, or pain to the nurse. Do not massage red areas or apply a new product without direction. Record the location and time of findings objectively.

Wheelchairs and walking aids support participation, but must be the right size and used according to the person's plan. Before use, check relevant parts such as brakes, the seat, footrests, and route. Devices do not all work the same way; follow training and the equipment instructions.

Walking assistance takes balance, fatigue, pain, and ability to follow directions into account. Someone who usually walks independently may need different assistance on a particular day. Activity is not a test of courage; allow rest and request an assessment if changes arise.

For an outing, plan the route, weather, toilet access, supervision, and rest stops. Hills, thresholds, and uneven paths require trained techniques for the equipment. Explain a change in movement before making it so the person is not startled.

Eating meets physical needs and can also be a social activity and source of enjoyment. Check that the food matches the person's identity under the facility system, diet, allergies, and assistance plan. Do not rely on seat location or how a plate looks to identify the recipient. The team should record and accommodate cultural and religious choices and habits.

Support for independence starts with the environment: table, utensils, lighting, and reach. A person may be able to eat independently if food is cut as planned or a particular utensil is prepared. Before assistance, check that posture, alertness, and swallowing ability match the assessment.

Explain the food and ask permission to help. Follow the person's pace; do not offer another spoonful while their mouth is still full. Observe responses such as difficulty, coughing, or fatigue and follow the reporting process. Do not force the person to finish a portion or mix all the food together just for efficiency.

Record the amount eaten according to facility practice, the type of assistance, any refusal, and concerns. Intake figures alone do not describe the mealtime experience; add observations that may help adjust the plan. If the food does not match the plan, confirm before serving it.

Swallowing moves food or liquid toward the digestive tract. Difficulty swallowing is called enge shōgai; material entering the airway is called goen, or aspiration. Report coughing during meals, a changed voice after swallowing, or repeated difficulty. The absence of coughing does not ensure that swallowing is safe. Swallowing assessments are done by qualified professionals.

The plan may specify positioning, food texture, liquid consistency, equipment, and level of assistance. Staff follow the individual plan and their training. Do not estimate thickness or amounts. Cutting food into smaller pieces is not automatically suitable for every swallowing difficulty.

sections.body:
If a new difficulty occurs during a meal, stop feeding, ensure safety, and call staff according to procedure. If the person cannot breathe or is unresponsive, use the trained emergency response. Do not force them to drink to “push down” food.

Hydration also follows the person's condition and plan. There is no single fluid target suitable for everyone, especially when clinical restrictions apply. Record intake using the facility system and report changes in drinking habits, dry mouth, or new concerns. Observations support communication; they are not a caregiver's diagnosis of dehydration.

Choice of equipment, positioning, and use of liquids must match the person's abilities and plan, especially if they have difficulty swallowing.

Watch for concerns such as pain, mouth sores, bleeding, dry mouth, or uncomfortable dentures. Report findings to the team; do not assume refusal to eat is always because the person dislikes the menu. Caregivers do not adjust dentures or perform dental procedures themselves.

Each person's dentures need identification, handling, storage, and cleaning products according to instructions and policy. Do not switch containers or casually use very hot water. When finished, record the assistance and any findings that need follow-up.

sections.body:
Elimination includes urination and bowel movements. Toileting support takes into account usual timing, mobility, clothing, communication, and privacy concerns. People who need assistance still have the right to an explanation and choices. Do not put everyone on the same schedule without considering their individual plan.

Independence can be supported with a safe route, easy-to-use clothing, toilet signs, and suitable equipment. Urgent needs can increase risk when a call bell is out of reach or the response is slow. The goal is not merely to prevent leakage, but to help the person stay comfortable and maintain routines where possible.

sections.body:
Before assisting with a transfer, check the plan, prepare hand-hygiene supplies and protective equipment, and explain each step. Once the person is in a safe position, protect their privacy while maintaining the supervision they need. Not everyone can safely be left alone; follow the assessment. Keep the call bell within reach and make sure the person knows how to use it.

Help with clothing and hygiene according to the person's abilities. When finished, check that they are comfortable, handle soiled items correctly, and clean your hands. Record the time and type of assistance. Report pain, new difficulty, or a change in pattern to the team.

sections.body:
Incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine or stool. It may make a person feel embarrassed and anxious about interacting with others. Caregivers should respond calmly, privately, and without blame. Do not call a person “dirty” or discuss leakage in front of others.

Absorbent products may help, but their type, size, checking frequency, and use must follow the plan. They do not automatically replace opportunities to use the toilet. The team needs to understand leakage patterns and barriers that can be addressed, not simply change the product after each incident.

sections.body:
Prepare supplies before starting so the person is not left uncovered. Protect comfort and cover body areas that are not being assisted. Keep clean and soiled equipment separate and follow trained hygiene techniques. Dry the skin gently; use skin protectant only as directed.

Check for concerns, redness, or visible skin changes during assistance and report new findings. After changing, make sure the product is not too tight, clothing is comfortable, and positioning follows the plan. Record the time, leakage, and assistance provided; do not independently restrict fluids to prevent leakage.

sections.body:
Elimination records help the team understand patterns and changes. They may include the time, frequency, amount if measured according to procedure, observed form or color, concerns, and type of assistance. Distinguish direct observations from what the person says. If an amount was not measured, do not write a number as if it were certain.

Constipation, diarrhea, or difficulty urinating requires assessment and a plan; caregivers do not choose medication or make a diagnosis. Report new changes, visible blood, pain, or a worsening condition according to the urgency procedures. Do not wait several days to collect notes when a sign needs an immediate response.

Use the terms or scale used by the facility after training. A note such as “bad bowel movement” is less useful than the time, observed form, and any concern. Also record whether the person declined assistance or could not reach the toilet in time.

Support with activity, diet, and fluids follows the individual plan. Do not give a laxative, change medication, or perform an invasive procedure because a record looks unusual. If the person feels embarrassed discussing elimination, explain why observations are needed and speak privately.

The person may feel uncomfortable because of cold, fear of falling, embarrassment, or a past experience. Explanation and consent help determine appropriate support.

Bathrooms present risks from wet floors, temperature changes, limited space, and transfers. Check equipment, routes, grab bars, and staffing needs under procedure. Check water and room temperature according to SOP and confirm with the person; do not rely only on how the staff member's hand feels or on one number without context.

Monitor their response throughout, including dizziness, pain, or fatigue. If their condition changes, stop and follow the reporting process.

After bathing, dry gently according to the plan, help the person dress, and make sure they are comfortable. Observe the skin when appropriate and with consent. Report new findings and record the assistance and response; completing the bath schedule alone does not show whether the activity was safe.

Seishiki (清拭) means cleaning the body by wiping. It may be part of the plan when a full bath is not suitable, but the decision follows the person's condition and team directions. Hygiene assistance still includes consent, privacy, comfort, and opportunities for the person to do the parts they can manage.

Prepare supplies according to SOP and keep clean and soiled equipment separate. There is no need to uncover the whole body for a long time to clean one area. Watch for cold, pain, and skin concerns. Products must match the plan, especially when the person has sensitivities or skin problems.

Do not cut an area that cannot be assessed properly, treat a wound, or perform a task outside your training. Report changes in skin or nails, and any concerns, to the relevant staff member.

sections.body:
Clothing relates to identity, comfort, culture, temperature, and planned activities. A person may have important preferences about color or style. Simple choices that are respected support participation. The need for physical assistance does not take away the right to choose one's appearance.

Check hand ability, seated balance, pain, and which parts of the clothing are difficult to use. Support may include laying out clothes, giving cues, helping with buttons, or assisting with part of a movement. For one-sided weakness, the general sequence of dressing the affected side first must be adapted to the plan and trained technique.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Prepare clothing before changing, close the door or curtains, and explain each step. Do not pull on a limb or force its range of motion. If clothing is difficult to use, discuss alternatives with the person and team instead of changing their preference without explanation.

After dressing, check for folds, tight areas, assistive-device placement, and comfort. Adjust shoes and footwear to the mobility plan as well. Offer a mirror or a chance to groom if the person wishes. Record the assistance needed so the next staff member can provide consistent support.

sections.body:
Sleep and rest are affected by routines, daytime activity, the environment, physical comfort, and worries. A person may be used to sleeping with a particular light or need help using the toilet at night. Support should consider these habits and the plan, rather than assume everyone should sleep at the same time.

Sleep observations include when the person appears asleep, waking, concerns, activities, and assistance. Record only what can be known; do not state an exact number of sleeping hours if the person was not observed throughout. New drowsiness or difficulty waking needs attention and reporting, not merely a note in the sleep record.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Prepare a comfortable environment with lighting and sound suited to the person's preferences and risks. Make sure pathways, the call bell, and assistive devices can be used. Night checks follow the plan and should minimize unnecessary disturbance where possible. Greet the person and explain before providing physical assistance.

If the person continues waking, ask about needs such as pain, toileting, temperature, or anxiety, then report patterns to the team. Do not give extra sleep medication or keep the person in bed as an independent decision. Discuss daytime activity support and sleep routines with the team.

Meaningful activities differ from person to person: gardening, music, reading, simple cooking, conversation, or spiritual activities. The aim is not to make everyone join the same activity. Consider each person's interests, life history, abilities, and wishes at the time. Refusing one activity does not automatically mean they do not want social contact.

Participation may mean doing part of an activity, choosing a song, observing, or helping decide the outcome. A simple activity can still provide a role and a sense of being valued. Avoid competition or praise that talks down to a person as if they were a child.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Check the activity risks and individual plan, including positioning, fatigue, equipment, and supervision needs. Offer real choices and do not force participation. Therapeutic movement exercises must follow a therapist's directions; caregivers do not create clinical exercise programs on their own.

Evaluate the person's experience, not just attendance. Ask whether they enjoyed the activity, watch for fatigue or discomfort, and record which support worked. A short activity the person enjoys may be more meaningful than a long session that causes distress.

Check lighting, pathways, temperature, noise, and access to belongings. Place the call bell, permitted drinks, glasses, and communication aids according to the plan and the person's abilities. Do not put items on a side they cannot reach just because it looks tidier.

sections.body:
The care process is a cycle of understanding needs, setting goals and a plan, providing support, and evaluating results. Caregivers contribute observations about daily activities and the person's preferences to the team. Needs are not assessed only by looking at limitations; remaining abilities and what the person wants to do are also important.

Goals should be understandable to the person and reviewable through observation. Instead of “everything gets better,” a goal might be that the person can choose clothes and put on certain items with suitable assistance. The plan explains the form of assistance, equipment, supervision level, and matters that need reporting.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Implementation follows the latest plan and the person's current condition. If the person refuses, develops a new concern, or the support method is ineffective, record it and discuss it with the team. Following the plan does not mean ignoring changes. Plan changes, in turn, are made through the team to keep support consistent and safe.

Evaluation compares goals with the response: what worked, what assistance is still needed, comfort, and the person's choices. Clear documentation gives a basis for adjustment decisions. Do not mark a goal as achieved merely because the activity was scheduled or staff finished helping.

sections.body:
Hōkoku means reporting results or changes to the person in charge. Renraku means sharing necessary information with relevant people. Sōdan means consulting someone when a decision or assistance is needed. These three practices are often summarized as hō-ren-sō. Information must be shared promptly, with the right person, through the appropriate channel.

Objective notes describe what can be observed or measured. A person's words may be recorded as a quotation, while assumptions must not be stated as facts. “At 12:10, said they felt nauseated and ate two spoonfuls” is more useful than “deliberately did not eat.” Avoid blaming labels or judgments about personality.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
For a report, organize the time, location, event, usual condition, actions taken, and response. If a decision is needed, state the question clearly. Share emergency information immediately; complete the record afterward. Do not wait until the end of the shift if a change needs a response now.

Use the official system and correct errors according to policy so the change history remains clear. Do not remove facts to make a report look better. Checking names and recipients helps prevent information from being entered under the wrong person.

sections.body:
Handover supports continuity of care between shifts. Include the person's condition, changes, assistance already provided, response, and anything outstanding. Give enough specific information for the next staff member to know what to monitor or do. Reading a note does not replace clarification when an important point is unclear.

An incident report describes the factual sequence and actions taken after safety is addressed. Report errors and near misses through the established procedure. Hiding an incident to protect a staff member's image can remove an opportunity to prevent recurrence and leave the team without important information.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
At handover, make sure the recipient understands priorities and outstanding tasks. Repeat safety-related points and confirm who is responsible. Protect privacy by choosing an appropriate place or system. Do not include gossip or labels that do not help with support.

Caregivers also need to maintain their readiness through rest, training, ergonomics, and emotional support. Report severe fatigue, injury, or limitations that may affect safety. Asking for help is part of professional responsibility, not a personal failure. Use supervisory channels when facing pressure or suspected abuse or neglect.

lessons.response: 左 means left. Confirm the concern by politely pointing or repeating what was said, then report the correct location. Do not guess which side of the body is affected.

sections.body:
Kaigo vocabulary should be learned in context. 右 (migi) means right, 左 (hidari) left, 手 (te) hand, 足 (ashi) foot or leg, and 腰 (koshi) lower back or waist. 痛み (itami) means pain, while かゆみ (kayumi) means itching. Do not replace one concern with another term when making a report.

Time and sequence often determine what to do: 前 (mae) means before, 後 (ato) after, 今 (ima) now, and 後で (ato de) later. 午前 (gozen) and 午後 (gogo) distinguish before and after noon. Number readings change in some combinations: 四時 is read よじ, 七時 is しちじ, and 九時 is くじ. Confirm the meaning by repeating it back, not just by recognizing kanji.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Practice reading short instructions: 食事の前に手を洗います means “Wash your hands before eating.” 右の足が痛いです means “My right foot/leg hurts.” Distinguish staff observations from the person's words by adding と話しています (“says that...”) when reporting a quotation.

For fluid amounts or other measurements, state the unit shown in the record and do not alter the number without a basis. 少し (“a little”) and 全部 (“all”) are not precise measurements. If you do not understand a number, body side, or sequence, repeat it to the person who gave the information and ask for confirmation. Make personal study cards from vocabulary in earlier lessons, then use the words in relevant sentences.

lessons.response: In this context, the person says they do not need help yet. Confirm their answer, respect their choice, and explain that help remains available if needed.

sections.body:
The pattern ～てもよろしいですか asks permission politely, for example, お手伝いしてもよろしいですか (“May I help you?”). The pattern ～ましょうか offers assistance, for example, カーテンを閉めましょうか (“Shall I close the curtains?”). Use clear sentences suited to the person, rather than long keigo expressions that are hard to understand.

For concerns, ask どこが痛いですか (“Where does it hurt?”) and いつからですか (“Since when?”). Listen without making a diagnosis. 大丈夫です may mean “I'm fine” or be a polite refusal of an offer; context and confirmation still matter. まだ means “not yet” or “still,” while もう can mean “already.” Misunderstanding these words can change the order of assistance.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Conversation example: staff member, “お手洗いに行きますか。” The person, “まだ大丈夫です。” Staff member, “分かりました。行きたくなったら教えてください。” This means: “Would you like to go to the toilet?” “I’m all right for now.” “Understood. Please tell me when you would like to go.” The response respects the person's answer while keeping help available.

Another example: the person says, “寒いです。” The staff member says, “寒いのですね。毛布をお持ちしましょうか。” This means: “I’m cold.” “You feel cold; shall I bring you a blanket?” If the concern is new or related to a clinical condition, report it to the team as required. The purpose of language practice is accurate communication, not simply memorizing translations.

sections.body:
Work notes often include the time, activity, assistance, the person's words, and follow-up. A made-up practice example: “12:10 昼食を半分食べた。吐き気がすると話した。看護師に報告した。” This means: at 12:10, ate half of lunch; said they felt nauseated; reported it to the nurse. The note does not state a diagnosis or confirm that all follow-up was completed.

A second example: “15:00 歩行中に疲れたと話した。椅子で休んだ。” This means: at 15:00, said they felt tired while walking; rested in a chair. During handover, staff still need to explain the response after the rest and any team instructions. 報告した means “reported”; it does not automatically mean a decision was received.
sections.title: Understand the Concept

sections.body:
Integrated case: a person chooses to eat independently, but today seems sleepier and has a new difficulty swallowing. Supporting independence remains important, but safety and the change in condition require stopping assistance and escalating according to procedure. Do not continue just because the person was previously independent.

Use the learned process: identify the person's baseline, listen to concerns, check the plan, seek consent, prepare assistance, observe the response, and report changes. After immediate needs are addressed, document the facts and follow-up. Completing a course shows that the material was studied and knowledge checks were done; practical competence is still assessed through workplace training and supervision.
